overview.text: Kashrut, also spelled kashruth, is the Jewish system of dietary laws and practices; “kosher” means fit or permitted under that system. Its scriptural foundations include the Torah’s classifications of animals, while rabbinic interpretation developed further rules for preparing, slaughtering, and serving food—so kosher status concerns more than ingredients alone. Distinctive rules include permitting land animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, allowing fish with fins and scales, and separating meat and dairy, often with separate utensils. Foods that are neither meat nor dairy are called pareve. Kashrut connects everyday eating with Jewish religious tradition, though observance and interpretation differ among Jewish communities.

key_facts.text: “Kosher” means “fit” or “proper”; it describes food permitted under kashrut.
The Torah provides kashrut’s scriptural foundations; rabbinic interpretation added rules about food preparation, slaughter, and separating meat and dairy.
Among the permitted foods, land animals must chew the cud and have split hooves; kosher fish have fins and scales.
Meat and dairy are kept separate, often using separate dishes and utensils; foods that are neither are commonly called pareve.

For meat to be kosher, the FAQ describes ritual slaughter called shechitah and removal of blood; it also notes that observance and discussion of kashrut have developed differently across Jewish movements.
